feedback: 'The constant movement is movement in action, and direction changes, such as backing away after bumping into something, can show sensitivity — the organism responding to its environment.'
'Watching real motion helps counter the idea that single cells are inert or too simple to be truly alive.'
activities.intendedInsight: Unicellular organisms are visibly alive — they move, respond to surroundings and feed — not merely static diagram labels.
learnerActions: View pond water or a prepared Paramecium sample under a microscope, or watch a video of live microbes if a microscope is unavailable.
Describe what you see the organism actually doing: how it moves, how it changes direction, any feeding.
Match each observed behaviour to a life process and the structure likely responsible.
Optionally watch a free-swimming 3D or video Paramecium to appreciate cilia motion and the organism's scale in water.
activities.title: Observe live pond microbes moving and feeding

feedback: 'A single cell must do every job itself; a muscle or nerve cell is specialised for one job and depends on other cells for the rest.'
'Many specialised cells let a larger organism do jobs more effectively and grow bigger than one cell could manage alone.'
activities.intendedInsight: Multicellular organisms share life's jobs among specialised cells (division of labour), which is a solution to a size/complexity problem; they are not simply enlarged single cells.
learnerActions: Place a single-celled organism side by side with a specialised multicellular cell (e.g. a muscle cell or nerve cell).
Explain what the single cell must do that the specialised cell does not — and vice versa.
Answer: 'What can a multicellular organism do that a single-celled one can't, and why does having many cells help?'
State why multicellular organisms are not just 'bigger versions' of single cells.
activities.title: Compare unicellular self-sufficiency with multicellular division of labour

feedback: For a correct structure→process match: confirm the link and restate the function briefly.
For a mismatch: point back to what the structure physically does (e.g. 'the contractile vacuole handles water balance, so it links to excretion, not movement').
In the role-play, prompt for mechanism: 'How exactly do you move with no legs? How do you avoid bursting?'
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can independently name adaptations, map them to the correct life process, and articulate the unicellular-vs-multicellular contrast.
learnerActions: Match each microbe structure to the life process it performs.
Sort a set of features into the seven life processes.
Answer short questions contrasting unicellular and multicellular organisms.
Optionally take on the role 'I am an Amoeba — ask me how I survive' and explain in your own words how the organism eats, moves and avoids bursting.
activities.title: Consolidation check: match structures, sort processes, and explain in role
